tldr: Leveraging the property that the initial noise space in Flow Matching naturally segregates by behavioral mode, this imitation learning method adaptively separates the initial noise distribution only at behavioral branching points, enabling nearly 100% controllable action mode selection without modifying the network architecture.
hero_caption: Overview of the proposed method, MOSS. (a) In a drawer-opening task, the approach trajectory is shared, and behaviors branch into two modes midway. (b) While conventional Flow Matching (FM) implicitly separates modes starting from a single isotropic Gaussian, MOSS estimates the local degree of multimodality (branching degree), contracts the mode-specific sources toward a shared Gaussian prior to branching, and separates them by mode at the branching point. (c) The velocity field network itself remains shared across all modes, steering the robot toward the desired behavior simply by controlling which noise distribution generation starts from.
overview:
In robotic manipulation, even with the exact same visual observation, multiple valid actions often exist—such as choosing whether to bypass an obstacle from the right or the left. Generative policies like Diffusion Policy and Flow Matching (FM) naturally capture these multimodal behaviors. However, which mode gets executed at runtime is left to random sampling of initial noise, posing a major practical challenge: users cannot reliably target and produce their desired behavior.

While explicit conditioning methods (e.g., using instructions to specify modes) have been explored, high-dimensional visual features often induce shortcut learning, where the model ignores the low-dimensional condition labels. This frequently leads to mode collapse, especially when training data is imbalanced. To address this, the authors focused on a geometric insight: in FM, where a deterministic ordinary differential equation (ODE) transports noise into action, the initial noise space itself inherently possesses distinct preimages that lead to each specific behavioral mode.

Under an ideal deterministic flow, the noise space separates cleanly. In practice, however, limited model capacity and data scarcity blur these boundaries. To solve this, the authors propose MOSS (Mode-Oriented Source Shaping). MOSS pre-places mode-specific Gaussians in the initial noise space and introduces adaptive source shaping: it estimates whether the robot is at a behavioral branching point, separating the noise distributions only when a branch occurs.

Evaluated across 6 simulated tasks and 3 real-world manipulation tasks, MOSS steered to the target mode up to 100% of the time while maintaining high task success. Even under a heavily imbalanced 10:90 dataset, MOSS recovered minority modes at a guidance rate exceeding 90%. On real robots, it outperformed mode-conditioned FM by 43.3 percentage points in guidance rate, demonstrating outstanding controllability.
contributions: Revealed, both theoretically and empirically, that in Flow Matching under deterministic ODE transport, the initial noise space naturally induces mode-dependent structures serving as preimages for each behavioral mode.

Proposed MOSS (Mode-Oriented Source Shaping), which adaptively shapes the source space by estimating the local degree of multimodality—explicitly separating the initial noise distributions at behavioral branching points while contracting them into a single shared Gaussian along common trajectories.

Achieved reliable selection of the desired behavioral mode at inference time simply by changing the sampling source, without inputting mode labels into the velocity field network and without introducing extra computational overhead during inference.

Demonstrated high robustness by recovering minority modes at over 90% guidance rate under an extreme 10:90 data imbalance, along with substantial gains in controllability during real-world robot manipulation.

sections.heading: Let the Initial Noise Decide Which Action to Take
sections.summary: While generative policies can model diverse behaviors, which behavior actually manifests is left to random sampling. Instead of conditioning the velocity field network, MOSS adaptively shapes the geometry of the initial noise (source) space, steering execution to the intended behavior on demand.
sections.details:
When a robot opens a drawer or grasps an object, there is rarely just one way to succeed. Recent policies based on Diffusion or Flow Matching (FM) capture such multimodal action distributions well, yet the actual trajectory executed at inference depends entirely on the standard Gaussian noise vector sampled at runtime.

To control this, explicit conditioning—such as language instructions specifying the target mode—is widely used. However, because robot visual observations are high-dimensional and tightly coupled with task progression, models easily learn shortcuts between visual inputs and actions, frequently ignoring low-dimensional condition labels. Particularly under imbalanced data, minority behaviors are rarely generated at all.

To overcome this, the authors revisited the generative process of FM itself. FM deterministically transports a trajectory from a noise distribution to a target action distribution along an ordinary differential equation (ODE). This implies that if output behaviors separate into distinct modes, distinct regions (preimages) corresponding to those modes must already exist within the starting initial noise space.

Guided by this intuition, the authors developed MOSS (Mode-Oriented Source Shaping). MOSS generates noise from separated, mode-specific Gaussians only during critical phases where behaviors branch, while collapsing them into a single Gaussian along common trajectories to share data representations. This design allows users to freely guide behaviors simply by choosing the initial noise component, without adding any architectural complexity to the generative network.

sections.heading: Conditioning the Policy or Structuring Latent Geometry?
sections.summary: We review prior work on modeling multimodal actions and source design in Flow Matching. MOSS distinguishes itself by explicitly embedding semantic mode structure directly into the source space, avoiding the shortcut issues seen in direct policy conditioning.
sections.details:
Related work can be organized into three main streams:

### Limitations of Multimodal Generative Policies
Extensive research has explored latent variables and Mixture of Experts (MoE), such as VFP and MARS, to better capture multimodal behaviors without collapse. However, these remain passive modeling approaches aimed at representing multiple modes; they do not allow an external human operator to actively select a specific target mode.

### Source Space Design in Flow Matching
Several works alter FM's initial source distribution away from the standard normal distribution. Examples include starting from past action history (A2A), visual features (VITA), or latent representations (LAFM). However, their primary goal is inference acceleration—shortening transport distance to enable 1-step generation—rather than semantic mode control. While recent approaches like SL-FM lift actions into an orthogonal space, the correspondence to user-desired modes remains implicit and requires post-hoc alignment.

### Differences from Explicit Conditioning
The most direct approach is feeding mode IDs or language instructions into the policy network, as seen in VLA models and PF-DAG. However, this often suffers from shortcut learning where the network ignores condition inputs. MOSS supplies zero mode information to the velocity field network, determining the mode entirely through the initial noise sampling location. This delivers robust controllability without compromising the network's representational capacity.

sections.heading: The Hidden Preimage Structure of Deterministic Flows
sections.summary: Under ideal ODE transport, the initial noise space naturally partitions into distinct regions corresponding to each behavioral mode. However, in practice, finite data and approximation errors blur these boundaries, triggering mode confusion and collapse.
sections.details:
This section provides the theoretical foundation for why FM enables mode control solely through noise space manipulation.

### 3.1 Noise Zoning and Geometric Regularity
In the action space, let $\mathcal{A}_k^{\mathbf{o}}$ be the region belonging to mode $k$. Given an ideal ODE flow map $\Phi_{\mathbf{o}}$ that transports initial noise $\mathbf{z}$ to the final action, the source-space preimage for each mode is $\mathcal{Z}_k^{\mathbf{o}} = \Phi_{\mathbf{o}}^{-1}(\mathcal{A}_k^{\mathbf{o}})$.

- **Theorem 1 (Noise Zoning)**: When the flow map is continuous and satisfies exact transport, these noise regions $\mathcal{Z}_1^{\mathbf{o}}, \dots, \mathcal{Z}_K^{\mathbf{o}}$ form mutually disjoint open sets, and the Gaussian probability mass of each region exactly matches the marginal probability of its corresponding mode.
- **Theorem 2 (Geometric Regularity)**: Under standard regularity conditions where the flow is a bi-Lipschitz homeomorphism, each noise region is connected. Stable actions located far from decision boundaries in action space retain wide safety margins (spherical neighborhoods) in noise space.

In short, even without intervention, distinct "territories" for each mode naturally exist in the noise space from the start.

### 3.2 Why Practical Boundaries Blur
In practical robot learning, however, transport errors $\eta_{\mathbf{o}}(\mathbf{z})$ inevitably arise due to limited demonstration data, finite network capacity, and few numerical integration steps.

When this error exceeds the semantic margin, the generated action strays outside its intended region, causing mode confusion, bias toward dominant modes, or outright mode collapse. Relying solely on the natural, unassisted partitioning of a standard Gaussian source is the fundamental reason traditional generative policies fail to offer controllable action selection.

captions.F2: LDA visualization of the initial noise space when training a standard FM policy on a multimodal task (2D Navigation). Even without explicit mode conditioning, the positions of initial noise vectors are biased according to which mode (Modes 1–4) they eventually reach, confirming that source-space mode separation emerges naturally. However, the boundaries between modes exhibit severe overlap.

sections.heading: Adaptive Source Shaping: Expanding and Contracting Noise Space
sections.summary: MOSS applies adaptive control: it pushes mode-specific initial noise distributions apart only when actions branch, and pulls them back to the center during shared trajectory segments. The framework introduces a lightweight multimodality estimator and a Gaussian placement algorithm based on a mode-discriminative subspace.
sections.details:
Building on theoretical insights, MOSS adopts an explicit and dynamic approach to source-space separation.

### 4.1 Overall Pipeline
In MOSS, initial noise $\mathbf{x}_0$ is sampled from a Gaussian source specific to mode $k$. Crucially, no mode label is fed into the single velocity field network $\mathbf{v}_\theta$. The network learns a unified transport shared across all modes, and behavioral differences stem purely from where in the noise space generation begins.

### 4.2 Modality-Strength Estimator
Behaviors do not diverge across the entire task horizon. For instance, when opening a drawer, the initial reaching phase toward the handle is identical whether pulling from the left or the right. To capture this, MOSS introduces a lightweight MLP $s_\phi$ that predicts the local degree of multimodality.

Using training data, the estimator retrieves neighboring samples with similar observation and action histories, computing a multimodality target $r_i$ based on the ratio between between-mode variance $\mathrm{Var}_B$ and within-mode variance $\mathrm{Var}_W$ over future action chunks. Trained on these targets, the estimator outputs a strength $q$ close to $1$ at branching points, returning near $0$ once branching concludes. At inference, a temporal persistence filter prevents sudden drop-offs in separation.

### 4.3 Adaptive Mode-Oriented Source Shaping
Based on the estimated strength $q \in [0, 1]$, MOSS dynamically adapts the geometry of the initial noise space.
Offline, it identifies the mode-discriminative subspace $\mathbf{U}$ along which future trajectories diverge. Source means $\bm{\mu}_k(q)$ for mode $k$ are positioned along this subspace. As strength $q$ increases, the inter-center distance expands and the variance $\sigma_\parallel(q)$ contracts to minimize overlap. Conversely, when $q$ is small during shared trajectory segments, all source distributions collapse into a standard Gaussian at the origin.

This mechanism allows the policy to fully share representation learning across all data during common actions, while steering the robot decisively toward the specified mode at branching points.

captions.F4: Progression of modality strength over the task horizon. Strength remains low during the initial drawer approach and post-grasp phases, peaking sharply only during the critical phase immediately before grasping (highlighted in orange) where trajectories diverge.

sections.heading: Decisive Mode Steerability Across Simulation and Real Robots
sections.summary: Across 6 simulation environments and 3 real-world setups, MOSS achieved up to 100% guidance rate (GR) while maintaining high task success rates (SR). Notably, it reliably recovered minority modes under a 10:90 data imbalance and substantially outperformed conditional baselines on real hardware.
sections.details:
Experiments thoroughly evaluated three core questions: (1) Does it accurately steer to the intended mode? (2) Can it recover minority modes from imbalanced data? (3) Does it improve task success rates and sample efficiency?

### 5.1 Experimental Setup
Simulations included four 2-mode tasks (Push Cube, Grasp Eyeglasses, Stack Cube, Put Wine) and two multi-mode tasks (2D Navigation, Place Cube). Real-world experiments were conducted on a Galaxea R1 Lite robot across three tasks: Place Cups, Pick Veg, and Open Drawer. Baselines encompassed unconditional policies (FM-DiT, DDPM-DiT, ACT, BeT, MARS, A2A), Mode-conditioned FM (feeding mode labels to the velocity field), and GMM-Sourced FM (using data-driven source mixtures).

### 5.2 Controllable Multimodal Behaviors
In simulation, unconditional models exhibited heavy mode bias or collapse. In contrast, MOSS delivered nearly 100% Guidance Rate (GR) alongside high Success Rates (SR) across all tasks. It demonstrated rock-solid controllability even on multi-mode tasks like 2D Navigation (4 modes) and Place Cube (3 modes).

Real-world results were especially striking. While Mode-conditioned FM suffered severe mode collapse on certain modes (GRs of 0%–15%), MOSS executed all modes in a balanced manner, achieving an average GR of 84.2% and an average SR of 85.3%. This outperformed Mode-conditioned FM by a dramatic margin of 43.3 percentage points in GR and 12.0 points in SR.

### 5.3 Robustness to Data Imbalance
Under an extreme 10:90 demonstration ratio, MOSS reached over 90% GR for the minority mode (10 demonstrations) in very few training steps. Because the shared velocity field effectively transfers shared trajectory structures from the majority mode, MOSS achieved far higher sample efficiency than FM-DiT trained from scratch exclusively on minority demonstrations.

### 5.4 Ablation Studies
The authors compared single-Gaussian partitioning, separation only at branching steps, unadapted separation (fixed source shaping), and adaptive MOSS. Structuring mode separation across chunks and adaptively shaping sources via modality strength proved essential for achieving both high guidance rates and rapid training convergence.

captions.F6: Success rate (blue) and guidance rate (green) of MOSS on tasks with three or more modes: 2D Navigation (4 modes) and Place Cube (3 modes). Beyond binary branching, MOSS achieves remarkably high success rates and around 90% accurate mode guidance across all specified modes in complex multimodal settings.
captions.F7: Learning curves for the minority mode (Mode 1) under a 10:90 imbalanced dataset. The horizontal axis represents the cumulative number of sampled minority demonstrations. MOSS (orange) attains high guidance rates with substantially fewer minority sample exposures compared to Mode-conditioned FM (teal) and FM-DiT trained only on minority data (blue).

sections.heading: Summary and Future Directions
sections.summary: MOSS introduces a fresh paradigm by structuring the geometry of the initial noise space, unlocking powerful mode control for Flow Matching policies. Extending beyond fixed, predefined discrete modes remains an open challenge.
sections.details:
This study uncovered the inherent mode-segregated preimage structure within deterministic transport models and introduced MOSS to explicitly leverage it through adaptive source shaping. Switching behavioral modes simply by selecting where noise is sampled—without altering network architectures or inference algorithms—represents an elegant, practical solution for robotics.

### Stated Limitations
The authors identify two primary limitations:
- **Predefined Discrete Modes**: The method assumes a fixed number of discrete modes defined prior to training, and does not directly support automatic discovery of unknown modes or continuous behavioral adjustments (such as smooth style tuning).
- **Application to Large-Scale VLAs**: While the principle applies to large Vision-Language-Action models, validating its behavior on multi-billion-parameter foundation models remains future work.

sections.heading: Appendix: Noise-Space Visualizations and Theoretical Grounding
sections.summary: The appendix empirically verifies that even standard FM exhibits mean shifts across modes in its initial noise space, complemented by rigorous mathematical proofs grounded in bi-Lipschitz continuity.
sections.details:
The appendix details preliminary experiments supporting the paper's theoretical claims.

### Verifying Noise-Space Bias in Standard FM
In the 2D Navigation task, the authors executed 1,000 rollouts using standard FM sampled from an isotropic Gaussian and analyzed the initial noise vectors of 939 successful runs. Calculating the mean noise value along the dimension corresponding to vertical movement yielded values of -0.303, -0.182, 0.135, and 0.286 for Modes 1 through 4, respectively—a monotonic trend matching the physical heights of the waypoints.

Furthermore, when new rollouts were seeded from Gaussians centered at these empirical mode means, the policy generated the intended mode with 62% probability for Mode 1 and 56% for Mode 4. This provides definitive evidence that loose mode zoning emerges naturally even in vanilla FM, strongly validating MOSS's approach of explicitly reinforcing this separation.

captions.F8: Comparison of guidance rates across training epochs between fixed source separation (MOSS fixed) and adaptive shaping (MOSS). Adaptive shaping (red and orange) consistently achieves higher guidance rates from early training stages, demonstrating an intrinsic advantage that does not depend on cherry-picked checkpoints.

takeaways: In deterministic generative policies like Flow Matching and Diffusion, starting positions in noise space are inherently tied to final behaviors, making source space geometry a powerful control knob.
Explicit conditioning that feeds labels or mode variables directly into policy networks is susceptible to visual shortcuts, often leading to mode neglect and collapse under imbalanced data.

Rather than separating modes throughout the entire horizon, adaptively separating the noise space only at behavioral branching points enables both shared representation learning on common trajectories and decisive mode guidance at branching points.

Mode control is achieved simply by switching the sampling source without Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG), vector field distortion, or extra inference computation, making it directly compatible with 1-step inference policies.
limitations: Requires behavioral modes to be annotated as discrete labels prior to training; cannot autonomously discover undefined modes or create new ones.
Extending the formulation to continuous mode control—such as smoothly varying movement velocity or grasp positions—remains an open challenge.

Evaluations were conducted on relatively compact imitation learning policies; verifying whether identical source shaping operates effectively on multi-billion-parameter Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models has not yet been performed.
